examinerBank.question: Given that this patient completed TB treatment 10 months ago and is now back with similar symptoms, walk me through your differential diagnosis and how his treatment history changes your thinking.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: The top differential must be drug-resistant TB relapse, given completed prior treatment with reported adherence gaps and muti use — both classic drivers of acquired resistance. Simple drug-susceptible relapse is possible but must be excluded by resistance testing, not assumed. HIV-associated bacterial pneumonia is less likely given the indolent 8-week course and marked constitutional symptoms. Post-TB bronchiectasis with secondary infection is possible given prior lung damage but doesn't explain active cavitation or the systemic symptoms as well. Malignancy is lower probability but relevant given HIV and weight loss. Crucially, any patient with a history of prior TB treatment must have GeneXpert with explicit assessment of rifampicin resistance sent as a priority, since retreatment cases have a substantially higher pre-test probability of drug resistance than new cases.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Full marks: explicitly identifies previous treatment as the key driver of resistance risk and ranks DR-TB first with clear reasoning, not just 'TB' undifferentiated. Partial: mentions TB without stratifying resistance risk.

examinerBank.question: Explain the mechanism by which this patient's lung has developed cavitation again despite completing treatment previously.
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Under sub-therapeutic drug pressure — from missed doses and possible interference from concurrent traditional muti use affecting absorption or metabolism — mycobacterial subpopulations with pre-existing or acquired resistance mutations (in this case a katG mutation conferring isoniazid resistance, plus rifampicin resistance) survive and proliferate while susceptible organisms are killed. This selects for a resistant bacterial population that continues to cause progressive caseous necrosis and cavity formation, particularly in the oxygen-rich, poorly-lymphatic-drained upper lobes.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the selection-pressure mechanism (incomplete killing selects resistant subpopulations) linked to specific patient risk factors (adherence, muti), not just 'the TB came back'.

examinerBank.question: The GeneXpert result shows rifampicin resistance detected. What does this mean practically, and what would you do next while awaiting full drug susceptibility testing?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Rifampicin resistance on GeneXpert is used as a proxy for MDR-TB in South Africa because roughly 90% of rifampicin-resistant strains are also isoniazid-resistant. This mandates immediate referral to the DR-TB programme, airborne isolation, and initiation of an appropriate all-oral second-line regimen without waiting for full culture-based DST, though the LPA and culture DST should still be sent to confirm the resistance pattern (including fluoroquinolone susceptibility, which determines regimen eligibility) and to detect any additional resistance.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Wants the candidate to know that treatment is not delayed pending full DST, and that rifampicin resistance triggers immediate programmatic action and isolation.

examinerBank.question: His HIV viral load comes back unsuppressed at 8400 copies/mL despite him being on ART. How does this affect your overall management plan?
examinerBank.modelAnswer: Unsuppressed viral load on ART suggests poor adherence (consistent with his history) rather than necessarily resistance, though HIV drug resistance testing could be considered if adherence is confirmed to be good. Management requires intensified adherence counselling for both his ART and his new DR-TB regimen, ideally with a single treatment supporter coordinating both, careful review for drug-drug interactions between second-line TB drugs (e.g., bedaquiline) and his ART regimen, and closer clinical and virological follow-up. Poor immune control also increases his vulnerability to other opportunistic infections and worsens TB treatment outcomes, so this must be addressed in parallel, not sequentially.
examinerBank.gradingNotes: Tests integration of HIV and DR-TB management — wants recognition of adherence as root cause, drug interaction awareness, and parallel rather than sequential care.

framework: chronic cough + constitutional symptoms with prior TB treatment history

patient.name: Sibusiso Mkhize
patient.personality: stoic, slightly defensive about his previous treatment, worried about losing his job if admitted again
patient.openingLine: Doctor, this cough is back again, worse than before... I don't understand, I finished my TB tablets already.

presentingComplaint: 8-week productive cough with weight loss, having previously completed TB treatment 10 months ago

history.fact: Cough began gradually about 8 weeks ago, initially mild, now constant and worsening
Completed a full 6-month course of first-line TB treatment (2HRZE/4HR) about 10 months ago at his local clinic, declared cured
Cough productive of thick yellow-green sputum, with blood streaking on and off for the past 2 weeks
Drenching night sweats most nights for the past month, has had to change bedding
Lost approximately 8 kg over 2 months, appetite poor, belt now on the tightest hole
Low-grade fevers most evenings, occasional chills, has not measured temperature at home
Increasing shortness of breath, now breathless walking to the taxi rank which used to be easy
Mild right-sided chest discomfort, worse with deep breaths or coughing, no radiation
Admits he sometimes missed doses toward the end of his last course because he 'felt better' and was working night shifts; also used traditional muti alongside tablets for a few weeks
No known current household TB contacts, but he shared a room with two other men at a previous work hostel where TB was common
Tested HIV positive 2 years ago, on ART (TLD) since then, says he takes it 'most days' but has missed clinic visits recently due to work shifts
Cannot recall exact TB drug names from last time but remembers 'a lot of tablets, some red urine'; unsure if he was tested for resistance at diagnosis
No other chronic illnesses, no diabetes, no previous hospital admissions besides TB treatment initiation
Currently only on ART (TLD); no other regular medication; occasional paracetamol for fever
Smokes about 5 cigarettes a day for 10 years, drinks alcohol socially on weekends, lives alone in a rented backroom in Umlazi, works night shifts as a security guard
No family history of TB or diabetes; father had hypertension
No headache, no vomiting, no diarrhoea, no urinary symptoms, no skin rash, no joint pains

examination.general: Thin, chronically ill-looking man, visibly tired. Mild pallor. No oral thrush. No peripheral lymphadenopathy. No clubbing, no cyanosis. Speaks in full sentences but pauses to catch breath.
examination.respiratory: Trachea central. Reduced expansion on right side. Right upper and mid zone: dull to percussion with bronchial breathing and coarse crackles. Occasional crackles left upper zone also. No pleural rub.
examination.cardio: Tachycardic, normal heart sounds, no murmurs, JVP not raised.

investigations.name: Line probe assay (LPA) for isoniazid and second-line resistance
investigations.result: katG mutation present (high-level isoniazid resistance); no fluoroquinolone resistance detected

investigations.name: Sputum culture and full drug susceptibility testing (DST)
investigations.result: Pending — MGIT culture positive at 3 weeks, confirms rifampicin and isoniazid resistance (MDR-TB), fluoroquinolone-susceptible

investigations.name: Chest X-ray
investigations.result: Bilateral upper lobe cavitating infiltrates, right greater than left, volume loss right upper lobe consistent with previous TB and new active cavitation

investigations.name: HIV viral load and CD4 count
investigations.result: Viral load 8400 copies/mL (not suppressed), CD4 count 246 cells/µL — suggests suboptimal ART adherence

investigations.name: Urea & electrolytes and creatinine
investigations.result: Normal — baseline needed before starting aminoglycoside/bedaquiline regimen

investigations.name: Liver function tests
investigations.result: Mildly elevated ALT 48 U/L, otherwise normal — baseline before hepatotoxic second-line drugs

investigations.name: ECG (baseline QTc)
investigations.result: QTc 410 ms — baseline required before bedaquiline/clofazimine due to QT-prolongation risk

differentials.dx: Multidrug-resistant pulmonary tuberculosis (relapse/reinfection with resistant strain)
for: poor adherence toward end of last course
HIV positive with unsuppressed viral load

against: GeneXpert confirms rifampicin resistance, which excludes simple drug-susceptible relapse
profound weight loss and night sweats
cavitating radiology atypical for simple bacterial pneumonia

differentials.dx: Post-TB bronchiectasis with secondary bacterial infection
against: active cavitation and confirmed rifampicin resistance points to active resistant disease rather than purely structural post-TB lung damage

differentials.dx: Pulmonary Kaposi sarcoma or other HIV-associated malignancy
against: GeneXpert positive with rifampicin resistance is the unifying and confirmatory finding

pathophys.cough with haemoptysis: Caseating granulomas and cavitation erode into the high-pressure bronchial arterial circulation supplying the lung parenchyma, causing brisk bleeding even from small cavities
pathophys.night sweats and weight loss: Mycobacterial antigen load drives macrophage release of TNF-alpha and IL-1, causing cytokine-mediated catabolism and hypothalamic temperature set-point dysregulation
pathophys.bilateral upper lobe cavitation despite: Incomplete eradication of Mycobacterium tuberculosis under sub-therapeutic drug pressure (missed doses, possible muti interference with absorption) selects for resistant bacterial subpopulations, particularly against rifampicin and isoniazid, allowing progressive cavitary disease
pathophys.dyspnoea on exertion: Progressive destruction of functional lung parenchyma from bilateral cavitating disease reduces the surface area for gas exchange, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and increased work of breathing
pathophys.low CD4 and unsuppressed viral load in a: Poor ART adherence allows ongoing HIV viral replication and progressive CD4 T-cell depletion, impairing granuloma formation and containment of mycobacterial infection, facilitating disease relapse and dissemination

staging: WHO HIV clinical stage 3 (pulmonary TB, on ART with virological failure); Rifampicin-resistant/MDR-TB (isoniazid and rifampicin resistant), previously treated patient, fluoroquinolone-susceptible on LPA

immediate: Isolate in airborne infection precautions (single room, N95 for staff) given confirmed rifampicin resistance
Notify as a drug-resistant TB case (notifiable medical condition, separate DR-TB register)
Assess for hospital admission criteria (hypoxia, haemoptysis, ability to self-isolate at home)
Baseline investigations before starting second-line regimen: FBC, U&E, LFTs, ECG (QTc), audiometry if aminoglycoside considered
definitive: Start all-oral short/modified regimen per SA DR-TB guideline (e.g. bedaquiline + linezolid + fluoroquinolone-based regimen such as levofloxacin, plus clofazimine/cycloserine per resistance pattern) under DR-TB clinical team supervision
Confirm regimen choice using full first- and second-line DST once available

Repeat HIV viral load assessment and step up adherence counselling; consider adherence support and possible regimen switch discussion with HIV clinician if genotypic resistance suspected on repeat testing
Continue/optimise ART concurrently with DR-TB treatment, monitoring for overlapping toxicities and drug interactions (e.g. dolutegravir with bedaquiline)
supportive: Nutritional support and consider grant/social worker referral given wasting
Enhanced adherence counselling addressing prior default and muti use, treatment supporter allocation
Contact tracing for recent close contacts (workplace hostel, current living situation) with symptom screening
Monthly monitoring for drug toxicity: renal function, LFTs, ECG/QTc for QT-prolonging agents, audiometry and visual acuity depending on regimen
Psychosocial support — DR-TB treatment is long and stigmatising; screen for depression/anxiety
followUp: Monthly sputum smear/culture conversion monitoring throughout DR-TB treatment
Regular ECG monitoring while on bedaquiline/clofazimine
CD4 and viral load monitoring on ART, consider adherence-focused counselling or resistance testing if viral load remains unsuppressed
Treatment duration per current SA DR-TB guideline (typically 9-11 months for short all-oral regimen if eligible, longer if not) with DR-TB clinical team review

stationChecklist.item: Introduces self, confirms patient identity, establishes rapport given sensitive treatment history
stationChecklist.why: Professionalism / communication, especially important with a patient who may feel blamed for relapse

stationChecklist.item: Characterises the cough fully: duration, sputum character, haemoptysis, progression
stationChecklist.answer: 8 weeks, productive yellow-green sputum, blood streaking for 2 weeks, progressively worsening
stationChecklist.why: Cough >2 weeks mandates TB workup; characterising haemoptysis identifies a red flag

stationChecklist.item: Screens constitutional symptoms: weight loss, night sweats, fever
stationChecklist.answer: 8 kg weight loss, drenching night sweats, evening fevers
stationChecklist.why: Core TB symptom screen per framework

stationChecklist.item: Specifically asks about previous TB treatment history, when, regimen, and outcome
stationChecklist.answer: Completed first-line 2HRZE/4HR about 10 months ago, declared cured
stationChecklist.why: Previous TB treatment is the single strongest risk factor for drug-resistant TB and must directly trigger resistance testing

stationChecklist.item: Explores adherence to previous treatment, including any traditional/muti use
stationChecklist.answer: Missed doses toward end of course, used muti alongside tablets
stationChecklist.why: Poor adherence is a key mechanism for acquired drug resistance — directly informs pathophysiology and risk stratification

stationChecklist.item: Asks HIV status, ART regimen, adherence, and last CD4/viral load
stationChecklist.answer: HIV positive 2 years, on TLD, admits inconsistent adherence and missed clinic visits
stationChecklist.why: HIV and unsuppressed viral load worsen prognosis and affect regimen choice and monitoring

stationChecklist.item: Asks about TB contacts (household, work, previous hostel)
stationChecklist.answer: No current household contacts, but shared hostel room previously where TB was common
stationChecklist.why: Identifies potential reinfection source and contact tracing targets

stationChecklist.item: Performs a full, focused respiratory examination including vitals/SpO2, inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation
stationChecklist.answer: SpO2 93%, RR24, right upper/mid zone dullness with bronchial breathing and crackles, reduced expansion right side
stationChecklist.why: Localises disease extent and quantifies severity/hypoxia per framework

stationChecklist.item: Explicitly screens for red flags: hypoxia, haemoptysis volume/severity, respiratory distress
stationChecklist.answer: SpO2 93% on room air, haemoptysis is streaking not massive, mild distress
stationChecklist.why: Red flag screening determines urgency of admission and isolation

stationChecklist.item: Generates a ranked differential explicitly considering drug-resistant TB given prior treatment, before committing to a diagnosis
stationChecklist.why: Symptom-to-differential reasoning is the exam philosophy; previous TB treatment must raise resistant TB specifically, not just 'TB relapse'

stationChecklist.item: Requests sputum GeneXpert Ultra (with explicit attention to rifampicin resistance result), line probe assay/culture DST, CXR, HIV viral load/CD4
stationChecklist.answer: GeneXpert: MTB detected, rifampicin resistance detected; LPA confirms isoniazid resistance too (MDR-TB)
stationChecklist.why: Confirmatory pathway per SA TB/DR-TB guidelines — rifampicin resistance result must be explicitly sought and reported

stationChecklist.item: Orders baseline investigations required before starting second-line DR-TB drugs: FBC, renal function, LFTs, ECG/QTc
stationChecklist.answer: Baseline bloods and ECG obtained — QTc 410ms, mild ALT elevation
stationChecklist.why: Bedaquiline, clofazimine and other second-line agents carry cardiac/hepatic/renal toxicity risks requiring baseline and monitoring

stationChecklist.item: Institutes airborne isolation precautions and notifies as a drug-resistant TB case
stationChecklist.why: Infection control and mandatory notification are immediate priorities once rifampicin resistance is confirmed

stationChecklist.item: Outlines appropriate all-oral second-line DR-TB regimen and coordination with the DR-TB programme/ART continuation
stationChecklist.why: Management must follow current SA DR-TB guideline framework, not standard first-line TB treatment

stationChecklist.item: Addresses contact tracing, adherence support/treatment supporter, and psychosocial factors given prior default
stationChecklist.why: Public health responsibility and relapse prevention given documented adherence problems
